decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: What is a motorist's highest duty on Missouri roads?
cards.back: A motorist's highest duty is careful, prudent driving, with speed and manner that keep the road safe for pedestrians, cyclists and other drivers as well as yourself.

cards.front: Does right-of-way law ever give a driver the right-of-way?
cards.back: Right-of-way law only says who must yield and never gives any driver the right-of-way, so you must do everything possible to avoid striking a pedestrian or vehicle no matter the circumstances.

cards.front: Where do right-of-way rules apply, and what do they decide?
cards.back: Right-of-way rules exist for places where vehicles or pedestrians are likely to meet and no signs or signals control traffic, and they say who goes first and who waits.

cards.front: Which governments can set traffic rules, and what can local rules cover?
cards.back: Cities, counties and the state can all set traffic rules, and you must obey each; local rules may set speed limits, one-way streets and stop signs, keep commercial vehicles off certain streets, control parking and turns, require signals, brake lights and horns, or ban sound-producing warning devices.

cards.front: What fines can speeding or passing in a state road work zone bring?
cards.back: Speeding or passing in a construction or work zone on Missouri state roads can bring a fine of at least two hundred fifty dollars for a first offense and at least three hundred dollars for any later offense, on top of other fines.

decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: How should you pass a pedestrian or a cyclist?
cards.back: Pass a pedestrian or cyclist with the same care as a motor vehicle, slowing and waiting for a safe chance just as you would behind any slow traffic.

cards.front: When may you pass on the right because of a left-turning vehicle or a wide city street?
cards.back: Passing on the right is allowed when the vehicle ahead is turning left or about to, or on a city street with clear pavement wide enough for two or more lines of vehicles each way.

cards.front: On which other roads may you pass on the right?
cards.back: Passing on the right is also allowed on a one-way street, or on a highway outside a city with clear pavement wide enough and marked for four or more lanes.

cards.front: How do the right-side passing rules differ between a highway outside a city and a city street?
cards.back: On a highway outside a city, passing on the right needs pavement marked for four or more lanes, while on a city street it needs room for two or more lines of vehicles each way.

cards.front: May you leave the paved roadway and use the shoulder to pass on the right?
cards.back: Passing on the right may never be done by leaving the paved main roadway and driving on the shoulder.

cards.front: Which places and road types add to the danger of passing?
cards.back: Intersections, vehicles inside an intersection and two-lane roads all add to the danger of passing.

cards.front: When must you avoid moving to the left side near a hill crest or curve?
cards.back: Do not move to the left side of the road when nearing a hill crest or curve where your view is blocked enough that an oncoming vehicle would create a hazard.

cards.front: Near which structures may you not drive left of center when your view is blocked?
cards.back: Do not drive left of center within one hundred feet of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel when your view is obstructed.

cards.front: Near which crossings, and with which line, may you not drive left of center?
cards.back: Do not drive left of center within one hundred feet of or at an intersection or railroad grade crossing, or anywhere a solid yellow line is present.

cards.front: Which two no-passing zones share the same distance?
cards.back: The same one hundred-foot distance marks two different no-passing zones on this page: near a bridge, viaduct or tunnel with an obstructed view, and near an intersection or railroad grade crossing.

decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: Whom do drivers yield to when crossing a sidewalk or using a driveway, and may you drive on a sidewalk?
cards.back: Drivers yield as needed to avoid hitting pedestrians crossing legally, and anyone crossing a sidewalk or entering or leaving a driveway, alley or parking lot yields to pedestrians; driving on a sidewalk is illegal except to cross it.

cards.front: Whom does a driver turning left yield to?
cards.back: A driver turning left yields to oncoming vehicles going straight.

cards.front: At a four-way stop, who goes first?
cards.back: At a four-way stop, the driver who reaches the intersection first goes first, after stopping completely.

cards.front: Entering a road from a driveway or alley, whom do you yield to?
cards.back: A driver entering a road from a driveway, alley or the roadside yields to vehicles already on the main road.

cards.front: At an intersection with no stop sign or signal, other than a roundabout, whom do you yield to?
cards.back: At an intersection with no stop sign or signal, other than a roundabout, yield to vehicles coming from your right.

cards.front: Approaching a roundabout, whom do you yield to before entering?
cards.back: Approaching a roundabout, yield to traffic already circulating and to pedestrians in the crosswalks, and wait for a gap before entering.

cards.front: Who goes first at a four-way stop, an uncontrolled intersection and a roundabout?
cards.back: A four-way stop goes by arrival order, an uncontrolled intersection goes to the vehicle on the right, and a roundabout goes to traffic already in the circle.

decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: How do you yield to an emergency vehicle using its siren and flashing lights?
cards.back: Yield to police, fire, ambulance and other emergency vehicles using a siren or air horn with a red or blue flashing light by pulling to the right edge of the road, or as near as possible, from whichever direction they come.

cards.front: What do you do if an emergency vehicle approaches while you are already in an intersection?
cards.back: If you are already in an intersection, drive through it before pulling over, stay stopped until the emergency vehicle passes, follow loudspeaker instructions, and move on only when the way is clear because more may follow.

cards.front: What should you do when nearing a stopped emergency vehicle on a road of four or more lanes?
cards.back: Nearing a stopped emergency vehicle showing red or red and blue lights on a road with at least four lanes and two or more going your way, move with caution into a lane not next to it if that is safe.

cards.front: What if moving away from a stopped emergency vehicle would be unsafe?
cards.back: If changing lanes away from a stopped emergency vehicle would be unsafe or impossible, slow down and keep a speed that is safe for conditions.

cards.front: How do the signals of a moving emergency vehicle differ from those that trigger the stopped-vehicle rule?
cards.back: A moving emergency vehicle you must pull over for uses a siren or air horn with red or blue flashing lights, while the stopped-vehicle rule is triggered by red or red and blue lights on a stationary vehicle.

decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: What light sequence does a school bus use before and at a stop?
cards.back: A school bus flashes amber warning lights five hundred feet before a designated stop, then shows alternating flashing red lights and its stop arm once stopped.

cards.front: What does the five hundred-foot figure mean for a school bus?
cards.back: The five hundred-foot figure is the distance before a stop at which a school bus starts its amber warning lights.

cards.front: On which roads must traffic stop for a school bus with red lights and stop arm on?
cards.back: When the bus's red lights and stop arm are on, oncoming and following traffic must stop before reaching it on a two-lane road with traffic both ways and on a two-lane one-way street.

cards.front: When do you not need to stop for a school bus with its red lights on?
cards.back: You need not stop when traveling the opposite way on a divided highway whose directions are on totally separate roadways, the opposite way on a highway of four or more lanes, or when the bus is in a school loading zone where students do not cross.

cards.front: What two things does the four-lane rule for school buses say?
cards.back: The four-lane rule for school buses cuts both ways: drivers going the opposite way on a highway of four or more lanes need not stop, and a bus may not load or unload where riders would cross more than two lanes of such a highway.

cards.front: After stopping for an unloading school bus, when may you go on?
cards.back: After stopping for an unloading school bus, watch for children along the roadside and stay stopped until the bus moves or its driver signals you on, then proceed with caution.

cards.front: How many points does a conviction for failing to stop for a school bus carry?
cards.back: A conviction for failing to stop for a school bus loading or unloading students carries five points.

cards.front: What suspensions apply for failing to stop for a school bus?
cards.back: Failing to stop for a school bus brings a court-ordered suspension of ninety days or as the court sets for a first offense, ninety days for a second offense within five years, and one hundred eighty days for a third or later offense within five years.

cards.front: At which offense does the school bus suspension double?
cards.back: The school bus suspension doubles only at a third or later offense within five years, to one hundred eighty days, while a second offense within five years stays at ninety days.

decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: When must you signal, and how?
cards.back: Signal before stopping, turning or changing lanes using hand and arm signals or your turn signals and brake lights, and check often that the vehicle signals work.

cards.front: How far before a turn must you be in the turn lane and signaling?
cards.back: Move into the proper turn lane and signal at least one hundred feet before a turn, and look both ways for oncoming traffic and pedestrians first.

cards.front: Why should you signal at least one hundred feet before turning?
cards.back: You should signal at least one hundred feet before turning so the drivers around you can get ready.

cards.front: With no signs or lane markings, which lane do you turn from and into?
cards.back: With no signs or lane markings, turn from the lane nearest the direction you are heading into the lane nearest the one you left, then change lanes afterward if needed.

cards.front: What can happen if you swing wide to the left before a right turn?
cards.back: Swinging wide to the left before a right turn can lead the driver behind to think you are turning left and pass you on the right.

cards.front: What should you avoid and allow for on a left turn?
cards.back: On a left turn, avoid cutting the corner into traffic coming from the left, but leave room for oncoming drivers to turn left in front of you.

cards.front: Turning from a one-way street onto a two-way street, where do you start and enter?
cards.back: Turning from a one-way street onto a two-way street, start in the left lane and enter to the right of the yellow dividing line, using the right lane of a four-lane road if it is free.

cards.front: Turning from a two-way street onto another two-way street, where do you keep your wheels and enter?
cards.back: Turning from a two-way street onto another two-way street, keep your left wheels as close as possible to the yellow line and enter to the right of the center line, using the right lane of a four-lane road if it is free.

cards.front: Turning from a two-way street onto a one-way street, where do you start and which lane do you enter?
cards.back: Turning from a two-way street onto a one-way street, start with your left wheel close to the yellow dividing line and, if the one-way road has two lanes, turn into whichever lane is free of traffic.

cards.front: With two left-turn lanes, which lane does each car enter?
cards.back: With two left-turn lanes, a car in the left-side turn lane enters the left lane just right of the yellow line, and a car in the right-side turn lane enters the right lane.
cards.memory_hook: left to left, right to right

cards.front: Where are U-turns never allowed?
cards.back: Make a U-turn only when safe, never on a curve or near a hill crest where others may not see you, never at a No U-Turn sign, and never at an intersection controlled by a signal or police officer; some towns ban them.

decks.domain: Missouri rules of the road: right-of-way, passing, emergency vehicles, school buses, signals, turns and roundabouts

cards.front: When may you use a center two-way left-turn lane, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Enter a center two-way left-turn lane only to slow or stop before a left turn from the main road, never travel in it more than five hundred feet, and never use it when entering from a side street.

cards.front: What is the most you may travel in a center two-way left-turn lane?
cards.back: The five hundred-foot figure is also the most you may travel in a center two-way left-turn lane.

cards.front: Which way do you travel around a roundabout, and whom do you yield to?
cards.back: At a roundabout you make a slight right turn and travel counterclockwise around the center island, yielding to traffic in the circle, bicyclists and pedestrians in the crosswalks.

cards.front: How should you approach a roundabout?
cards.back: Slow down before a roundabout, follow signs and markings to the correct lane in a multi-lane one, look left as you approach, and never make a left turn to enter.

cards.front: How should you drive once you are inside a roundabout?
cards.back: Inside a roundabout stay right of the center island, remember circulating vehicles have the right-of-way, and do not stop except to avoid a crash, change lanes or pass any vehicle.

cards.front: How should you leave a roundabout?
cards.back: Leave a roundabout at a slow speed with your right turn signal on, and do not speed up until you are past the exit's pedestrian crossing.

cards.front: What do you do about an emergency vehicle near a roundabout?
cards.back: Do not enter a roundabout when an emergency vehicle is approaching, and if one comes while you are inside, exit immediately and pull to the right.

cards.front: Why do roundabouts lower fatal and injury crashes?
cards.back: Roundabouts lower fatal and injury crashes by cutting speeds and removing left turns across opposing traffic, and every entering leg has a yield sign.

cards.front: What do you do if you miss your roundabout exit, and how do you treat trucks?
cards.back: If you miss your exit in a roundabout, keep circling until you reach it, and give trucks and trailers room because they may use more than one lane.

cards.front: What is a truck apron, and who may use it?
cards.back: A truck apron is the paved inner area of a roundabout for the rear wheels of large trucks, and cars, SUVs and pickup trucks must not use it.

cards.front: How does a J-turn intersection replace a left turn across fast traffic?
cards.back: At a J-turn intersection on a four-lane highway, instead of crossing fast traffic you turn right with traffic, merge to the far left lane, and then turn left in the direction you want to go.

recap_hooks.text: Your highest duty is careful, prudent driving, and right-of-way law only says who must yield.
State and local governments both set rules, and work zone speeding or passing adds fines of two hundred fifty dollars and up.
Pass on the right only for a left turner, on a wide city street, a one-way street or a four-lane highway, and never on the shoulder.
Stay right of center near blind crests and curves, and within one hundred feet of bridges, tunnels, intersections and railroad crossings.
Pass people on foot or on bikes with the same care as a car.
Left turns yield to oncoming traffic, and driveway drivers yield to the main road and to pedestrians.
Four-way stops go by arrival, uncontrolled intersections go to the right, and roundabouts go to traffic already circling.
For a siren and flashing lights, clear any intersection, then pull right and stay stopped until it passes.
For a stopped emergency vehicle, move over a lane if safe, or slow down if you cannot.
Amber lights start five hundred feet before a bus stop, and red lights with the stop arm mean stop on two-lane roads.
Opposite traffic on divided or four-lane highways need not stop, and you wait for the bus to move or wave you on.
Passing a stopped bus costs five points and suspensions that reach one hundred eighty days at a third offense.
Signal every stop, turn and lane change, and be in the turn lane signaling one hundred feet ahead.
Turn from the nearest lane into the nearest lane, without swinging wide or cutting corners.
Skip U-turns on curves, near hill crests, at No U-Turn signs and at signal-controlled intersections.
Use the center left-turn lane only to slow and turn, for no more than five hundred feet.
In a roundabout go counterclockwise, yield to circling traffic, keep off the truck apron and exit slowly with a right signal.
Clear a roundabout for emergency vehicles, and at a J-turn go right, merge left, then turn left.
